extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator; writers/readers of moral and social essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative remarks relevant to composing or appreciating short moral/social character sketches and light essays in the Spectator tradition (emphasis on character, atmosphere, and small comic particulars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for odd and uncommon characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Odd and uncommon Characters are the Game that I look for, and most delight in.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator explicitly values novelty in persons: unusual, singular characters provide the material that most delights and engages. Example/context: the author listens with 'more than ordinary Attention' to such a person, implying that selecting eccentric or novel figures is a deliberate approach to produce engaging copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through small habits and objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of minute, quirky details and domestic manufactures to define a person's character (e.g. carrying a tulip-root, exchanging a poppy, knitting garters, making nets, presenting shuttlecocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, idiosyncratic actions and objects (gifts, handicrafts, habitual questions like 'how they wear?') make a character vividly appealing and comic: 'These Gentleman-like Manufactures and obliging little Humours, make Will. the Darling of the Country.' Similarly, Sir Roger's parish eccentricities (lengthening a verse, pronouncing Amen repeatedly, counting the congregation) serve as small comic particulars that reveal personality and social role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dress and accoutrements to locate and define characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider 'the Force of Dress; and how the Persons of one Age differ from those of another, merely by that only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costume and accoutrements (broken lance, base-viol, petticoat shapes, buttons, boots, slashes) are powerful, economical signals of era, rank, temperament, and occupation. Dress can be used for comic contrast or to situate a portrait historically and socially (e.g. how the Yeomen's habit makes them look 'a Foot taller').

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating atmosphere for ghostly or affecting scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Select landscape and sensory details that naturally 'raise Seriousness and Attention' and make a scene proper for apparitions: ruins of an abbey, a long walk of aged elms, rooks and crows, ivy and elder-bushes, vaults and echoes, graves, dusk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembling these elements produces a setting in which audiences readily expect supernatural occurrences; the author notes that such objects and sounds 'naturally raise Seriousness and Attention' and that night intensifies the place's awfulness. Use of these concrete elements is recommended when the aim is to evoke terror, melancholy, or the uncanny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of belief by associative repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Locke: 'The Ideas of Goblins and Sprights have really no more to do with Darkness than Light: Yet let but a foolish Maid inculcate these often on the Mind of a Child...' — repeated association makes ideas inseparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To explain (or to create) popular superstitions and fears, emphasize how repeated pairing of unrelated ideas (darkness + goblins) in upbringing or discourse cements long-lasting associations. This principle can be used to account for credulity or to craft convincing superstition in narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose: use strange tales to encourage virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of apparitions and strange incidents serve a moral end: 'who by Instances of this Nature are excited to the Study of Virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting ghostly or remarkable tales, the narrator defends them on the grounds that such instances motivate virtuous behaviour; thus, including a moral lesson or showing social utility can justify entertaining or dubious anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect from affectionate, mildly ridiculous particularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Eccentricities that might be ridiculous in isolation are rendered amiable by the subject's general goodness and the author's affectionate framing (e.g. Sir Roger waking nodders, counting the congregation, giving hassocks and prayer books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray eccentric behaviour within a context of 'general good Sense and Worthiness' so that these particulars function as endearing foils rather than outright condemnations. This balance yields gentle satire rather than harsh ridicule.
